facts.text: The applicant is a Turkish national of Kurdish origin, resident in Diyarbakır, and wife of Mr Ali Tekdağ who disappeared in Dağkapı on 13 November 1994.

anchor.surface_text: 8.  The applicant is a Turkish national of Kurdish origin, resident in Diyarbakır. She is the wife of Mr Ali Tekdağ (A.T.), who disappeared in Dağkapı (Turkey) on 13 November 1994.

facts.text: On 13 November 1994 at about 11.00 a.m. the applicant and her husband went shopping in Küçükkadı, Diyarbakır; at Dağkapı, A.T. left her to attend to something and was followed by people with walkie-talkies and guns.

anchor.surface_text: 11.  On 13 November 1994 at about 11.00 a.m. the applicant and her husband A.T. went shopping in the village of Küçükkadı, in Diyarbakır. When they got off the bus at Dağkapı A.T. told the applicant that he had to attend to something and that she should wait for him for about five minutes. He went off in the direction of the bus station.

facts.text: A.T. returned less than two minutes later, walked past the applicant without looking, told her not to come near, made hand signs, and walked into a nearby street while being followed by armed people.

anchor.surface_text: 12.  A.T. returned less than two minutes later but, instead of coming to meet the applicant, he walked right past her without looking at her. When she called out to him, he said: “Don't come near me!”, made signs with his hands and walked into a street nearby. He was being followed by people with walkie-talkies and long-barrelled guns.

facts.text: Gunfire occurred; plain-clothed policemen arrived, took A.T. into a nearby building, then away in a white minibus; A.T. was bleeding from a head wound; soldiers nearby did not intervene.

anchor.surface_text: 13.  There was gunfire and everyone, the applicant included, threw themselves to the ground. When the firing stopped, plain-clothed policemen arrived on the scene. They took A.T. into a nearby building and a few minutes later took him away in a white minibus. A.T. was bleeding from a head wound received when he threw himself to the ground. There was a military vehicle parked in front of a bank near the scene, but the soldiers inside did not intervene.

facts.text: The applicant has not seen her husband since he was taken away by the police on 13 November 1994; she alleges witnesses saw him in custody but were afraid to testify.

anchor.surface_text: 14.  The applicant has not seen her husband since he was taken away by the police on that day. She alleges that a witness, Mr Seyfettin Demir, saw A.T. in custody at the Diyarbakır Headquarters of the Rapid Intervention Force while he himself was being held there and that in November 1994 other witnesses had seen A.T. in custody but were afraid to testify.

facts.text: On 16 November 1994 the applicant petitioned the Principal Public Prosecutor at Diyarbakır State Security Court for news of her husband but was initially turned away by police; she continued daily petitions for thirty days until meeting the prosecutor.

anchor.surface_text: 15.  On 16 November 1994 the applicant petitioned the Principal Public Prosecutor at the Diyarbakır State Security Court for news of her husband, but was turned away by the police. She continued to submit petitions every day for thirty days until she was at last taken to see the Principal Public Prosecutor, Mr Bekir Selçuk.

facts.text: The applicant reported her husband's disappearance to the prosecutor Mr Bekir Selçuk who said he would deal with it; later he said he had no information and denied security forces could have abducted A.T.

anchor.surface_text: 16.  The applicant reported her husband's disappearance to Mr Selçuk who said he would deal with the matter. When she returned a few days later, he said he had yet to obtain information. The applicant explained that, according to an article in Özgür Gündem newspaper, witnesses had seen her husband in prison but they were afraid to testify. She indicated that Seyfettin Demir was, however, willing to make a statement. Mr Selçuk replied that he wanted to know the names of the other witnesses, adding that the security forces could not have abducted her husband.

facts.text: A.T. had been taken into custody by Turkish security forces 19 times, imprisoned 17 times, and had changed identity to avoid recognition.

anchor.surface_text: 19.  A.T. had previously been taken into custody by the Turkish security forces 19 times, on 17 of which he had been put in prison. He had changed his identity and assumed the name Mehmet Aslan to avoid being recognised, arguing that the police detained him whenever they saw the name “Tekdağ”.

facts.text: About seven months after A.T.'s disappearance, policemen raided the applicant's house; she could not identify the persons but thought they were plain-clothed police officers.

anchor.surface_text: 20.   About seven months after A.T.'s disappearance, policemen raided the applicant's house.

facts.text: The first written request for investigation into A.T.'s disappearance was signed by his mother on 5 January 1995 and forwarded through authorities to Diyarbakır Police Headquarters, which denied custody on 9 January 1995.

anchor.surface_text: 21.  The first written request for an investigation into A.T.'s disappearance was signed by his mother and dated 5 January 1995. The request was addressed to the Provincial Governor of Diyarbakır, who forwarded it to the State of Emergency Bureau, which sent it to the Diyarbakır Police Headquarters. The latter issued a reply on 9 January 1995 denying that A.T. had been taken into custody.

facts.text: A.T.'s illegal change of identity could indicate he was still using a false identity and had joined the PKK terrorist organisation.

anchor.surface_text: 23.  A.T.'s illegal change of identity could indicate that he was still using a false identity and had joined the PKK terrorist organisation.

facts.text: The applicant's daughter was arrested on 7 November 1995 on charges of aiding and abetting the PKK.

anchor.surface_text: 24.  The applicant's daughter was arrested on 7 November 1995 on charges of aiding and abetting the PKK.

facts.text: An investigation into the death of the applicant's brother showed he had been assassinated by the terrorist group Hizbullah.

anchor.surface_text: An investigation into the death of the applicant's brother showed that he had been assassinated by the terrorist group Hizbullah.

facts.text: On 21 January 1996 the Evrensel newspaper published news from an anonymous source alleging A.T. was murdered in custody at Silvan Armoured Brigade barracks; the editor refused to disclose the source.

anchor.surface_text: 25.  On 21 January 1996 the Evrensel newspaper published some news, issued by an anonymous source, according to which A.T. had been allegedly murdered while in the custody of the Armoured Brigade barracks in Silvan. The editor of the newspaper, interrogated on this point by the Public Prosecutor of Silvan, refused to disclose the identity of the source.

facts.text: The main investigation file on A.T.'s disappearance contains 108 documents including judicial instructions, security forces information, and judicial decisions.

anchor.surface_text: 26.  The main investigation file concerning A.T.'s disappearance contains 108 documents, including instructions by the judicial authorities to the security forces to investigate, information provided by the security forces to the public prosecutors, and judicial decisions.

facts.text: The applicant submitted statements on 11 February 1995 and 22 March 1997 regarding her husband's disappearance.

The Diyarbakır Public Prosecutor's preliminary investigation file no. 1998/130 contains 108 documents and incorporates six previous investigation files, mostly ended with decisions of no jurisdiction or discontinued prosecution.
The Court held a hearing in Ankara on 13 and 14 October 2000 and took oral evidence from nine witnesses including the applicant, prosecutors, police officers, and others.

anchor.surface_text: 30.  The Court held a hearing in Ankara on 13 and 14 October 2000 and took oral evidence from nine witnesses.

facts.text: The applicant repeated her statements and alleged intimidation by State agents; she could not identify the persons who raided her house but thought they were plain-clothed police officers.

anchor.surface_text: 31.  The applicant repeated her previous statements. As regards her allegation that she had been intimidated by State agents on account of her application, she said she could not identify or describe the persons who had raided her house at night. She thought they were plain-clothed police officers.

facts.text: Mr Bekir Selçuk, Principal Public Prosecutor at Diyarbakır State Security Court, did not remember meeting A.T. or investigating his disappearance and found it inconceivable security forces would detain someone without informing the prosecutor.

anchor.surface_text: 32.  Mr Bekir Selçuk was the Principal Public Prosecutor at the Diyarbakır State Security Court at the time. He did not remember having met A.T. or having carried out an investigation into his disappearance. He said that no incident involving gunfire such as the one described by the applicant had been referred to him or to his office on the date of the alleged incident. He found it inconceivable that members of the security forces would detain someone without informing the public prosecutor. During his two meetings with the applicant, he had merely informed her that her husband had not been taken into police custody in connection with a case that was being dealt with by his office.

facts.text: Mr Hasan Şakrak, Public Prosecutor in Diyarbakır since 1999, conducted the investigation but had testimonies only from applicant and daughters, no references to other witnesses; he had not received all documents and never heard of Seyfettin Demir.

anchor.surface_text: 33.  Mr Hasan Şakrak was the Public Prosecutor in Diyarbakır who had been in charge of the case since 1999. It was he who had conducted the investigation into the disappearance of A.T. and into the alleged intimidation of the applicant by police officers. His investigation file only contained testimonies from the applicant and her daughters, Yasemin and Remziye, in which they made no references to the other people who had allegedly witnessed both incidents. Mr Şakrak said that a large part of the documents concerning A.T. had never been handed over to him. He had never heard of Seyfettin Demir and the documents concerning Mr Demir were not in his investigation file.

facts.text: Mr Ramazan Sürücü, Director of Anti-Terrorism Branch of Diyarbakır Police, denied A.T. was taken into custody by his unit and stated A.T.'s brother was abducted and killed by Hizbullah.

anchor.surface_text: 34.  Mr Ramazan Sürücü was the Director of the Anti-Terrorism Branch of the Diyarbakır Police Headquarters at the time. He had no idea what role Seyfettin Demir had played in A.T.'s disappearance. He denied that A.T. had been taken into custody by his unit. He also stated that A.T.'s brother had been abducted and killed by Hizbullah and that his team had caught the killers.

facts.text: Mr Ahmet Duran Alp, head of Rapid Intervention Force, said he had never heard of A.T.

anchor.surface_text: 35.  Mr Ahmet Duran Alp was the head of the Rapid Intervention Force at the time. There were approximately 400 uniformed officers in these units. He said he had never heard of A.T.

facts.text: Mr Necmi Çakar, head of Interrogation Unit of Anti-Terrorism Branch, said A.T. had been taken into custody and interrogated for PKK links; officers could use civilian vehicles including minibuses.

anchor.surface_text: 36.  Mr Necmi Çakar was the head of the Interrogation Unit of the Anti-Terrorism Branch in Diyarbakır, under Mr Ramazan Sürücü's orders. He said that A.T. had been taken into custody on various occasions and interrogated in connection with his links to the PKK. Mr Çakar knew that members of Hizbullah had murdered A.T.'s brother. He said that officers from the Interrogation Unit could use ordinary police cars and vehicles, including minibuses, with civilian number plates.

facts.text: Mr Hasan Şenay, Deputy Director of Diyarbakır Police Headquarters, signed letters indicating A.T. had not been taken into police custody at the alleged time, consistent with police custody registers.

anchor.surface_text: 37.  Mr Hasan Şenay was the Deputy Director of the Police Headquarters in Diyarbakır. He had signed two letters to the applicant, indicating that A.T. had not been taken into police custody at the alleged time (the letters were not produced by the Government to the Court). The letters were consistent with the information contained in the police custody registers that were sent to the Headquarters by all the police departments.

facts.text: Mr Kürşat Kılıçarslan, sergeant and head of Pirinçlik Gendarme Station, had no idea who A.T. was and did not remember the name.

anchor.surface_text: 38.  Mr Kürşat Kılıçarslan was a sergeant and head of the Pirinçlik Gendarme Station at the time. His deputy's name was G. Alp. It was gendarme practice to take statements from persons connected with incidents that occurred in their area of jurisdiction. The witness had no idea who A.T. was and did not remember the name.

facts.text: Mr Münir Büyükelçi, Public Prosecutor in Silvan, investigated A.T.'s disappearance, took statements, requested tracing of police officers and witness Seyfettin Demir, but received no replies and transferred file to Diyarbakır Public Prosecutor.

anchor.surface_text:
39.  Mr Münir Büyükelçi was the Public Prosecutor in Silvan, and had for a certain period been responsible for the investigation into A.T.'s disappearance. He had taken a number of steps to elucidate the facts. He had taken statements from the complainants and from the editor of the Evrensel newspaper on A.T.'s alleged murder while in the custody of the Armoured Brigade barracks in Silvan. 

Mr Büyükelçi said that he had begun a serious in-depth investigation but, having received no replies to his queries, he had transferred the file to the Diyarbakır Public Prosecutor. By letters of 6 May 1996 and 21 June 1996, he had invited the Diyarbakır Public Prosecutors' Office to trace the police officers who had been on guard in the vicinity of the incident venue and also to trace the main alleged witness, Mr Seyfettin Demir (see paragraph 39 above). Mr Büyükelçi never received a reply to his requests. Moreover, the information about Seyfettin Demir being in prison in Diyarbakır in 1994 was never transmitted to him (ibid.).
